canonicalExplanation.summary: Git has no single "undo"; pick the tool by **what you want to keep**. Discard working-tree edits to a file: `git restore file`. Unstage but keep edits: `git restore --staged file`. Undo a commit that's **already shared**: `git revert <hash>` adds a **new commit** that reverses it, so history stays intact for everyone. Move a branch back on **unpushed** local work: `git reset` (`--soft` keeps changes staged, `--mixed` keeps them unstaged, `--hard` **discards them**). Lost a commit after a reset? `git reflog` lists where HEAD has been, so you can recover it. Before anything destructive, run `git status` and consider a backup branch.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A commit that breaks checkout was merged to main an hour ago, and teammates have already pulled it. A learner runs `git reset --hard HEAD~1` and force-pushes. Now everyone's main disagrees with the server's. A bad commit already on main is undone with a new revert commit, preserving public history and reviewability. In this lesson you'll recover staged, committed and lost-ref mistakes in disposable repositories without overwriting shared history.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Issues, pull requests and review**, **Debugging and quality automation**, **Working tree, index and HEAD**, **Push and non-fast-forward rejection** and **Log, show and graph**.

sections.heading: The rule: choose by the state to preserve
sections.body:
```bash
git restore app.js              # discard unstaged edits to app.js (gone for good).
git restore --staged app.js     # unstage; edits stay in the working tree.

git revert 4c1e2f9              # new commit that reverses 4c1e2f9 (safe when shared).

git branch backup               # safety net before rewriting local history.
git reset --soft HEAD~1         # undo last local commit, keep changes staged.
git reset --hard HEAD~1         # undo it and DISCARD its changes.

git reflog                      # HEAD@{1}: the commit before the reset.
git branch rescue HEAD@{1}      # recover it onto a branch.
```

| I want to... | Use | Safe on shared history? |
|---|---|---|
| drop file edits. | restore. | n/a (local). |
| unstage. | restore --staged. | n/a (local). |
| undo a pushed commit. | revert. | yes. |
| rework unpushed commits. | reset --soft/--mixed. | only if unpushed. |
| find "lost" commits. | reflog. | n/a (local). |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Can reflog recover uncommitted edits destroyed by reset --hard?", "answer": "No. Reflog tracks where refs pointed, so it recovers commits. Edits that were never committed (or at least staged) are usually unrecoverable, which is why --hard needs care."}
```

examples.title: Reverting a bad commit on main
examples.situation: A bad commit already on main is undone with a new revert commit, preserving public history and reviewability.
walkthrough: **A bad commit already on main:** 4c1e2f9 broke checkout and has been pulled by teammates.
**Undone with a new revert commit:** git revert 4c1e2f9 creates "Revert 'Change cart rounding'", opened as a PR.
**Preserving public history and reviewability:** nobody's clone disagrees with the server, and the revert will be reviewed like any change.
examples.result: Checkout works again, and everyone's history stays consistent.

examples.title: The accidental reset
examples.situation: A learner runs git reset --hard HEAD~3 on a local branch, then realises two of those commits were needed.
walkthrough: git reflog shows HEAD@{1} pointing at the old tip.
git branch rescue HEAD@{1} restores those commits onto a branch.
Cherry-pick or reset back to recover the work.
examples.result: The commits are back within a minute, thanks to reflog.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Git undo is one universal command, and hard reset is the fastest safe way to reverse any mistake.
misconceptions.correction: Each tool preserves different state. Hard reset discards uncommitted work and rewrites history, which breaks shared branches; revert is the safe undo for published commits.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, why did everyone's main disagree with the server's?

analogy.example: Undoing in Git is like **correcting a shared ledger**. You never tear out a page others have copied (reset shared history); you add a correcting entry (revert). On your own scratch pad, you can erase freely (reset). And the ledger's audit trail (reflog) shows where pages went.
limitations: Scratch-pad erasing can still destroy uncommitted notes.
Audit trails expire eventually (reflog entries age out).

nearTransfer.prompt: In a disposable repo, practise each: discard an edit with restore, unstage with restore --staged, undo a commit with revert, undo a local commit with reset --soft. Show git status and git log after each.

farTransfer.prompt: In a sandbox, reset --hard away three commits, recover them with reflog onto a branch, then write a one-page "undo decision guide" for your team with the right command for each situation.

remediation.explanation: Before undoing, answer two questions: **what do I need to keep?** and **has this been pushed?** Pushed means revert; unpushed means reset is allowed, with a backup branch first.

recap.summary: To recover mistakes safely, use restore for working-tree edits, restore --staged to unstage, revert for commits already shared, reset only on unpushed history (knowing --hard discards changes), and reflog to find lost commits, never rewriting shared history to undo a mistake.
